summary: This historical review traces High Performance Fortran from its precursors (Fortran D, Vienna Fortran and CM Fortran) through the HPF 1.0, 1.1 and 2.0 standards and the HPF/JA dialect. It analyzes why HPF lost most of its user base despite influencing later languages such as Chapel, Fortress and X10.
why_read: It explains, from people who built the language, how distribution-based data-parallel compilation was expected to work and why it did not carry the field.
main_contribution: An account of the design decisions, the standardization process and the reasons for HPF's limited adoption, with lessons for future data-parallel languages.
main_limitation: The paper is a retrospective with no measurements of its own, and its causal analysis is interpretive.
